title: Tightest Window With K Ones
statement:
You get a binary string s and a positive integer k. Look at every contiguous substring that contains exactly k ones.

Among them, take the shortest. If several are equally short, return the alphabetically smallest one (compare as strings, so "1011" < "1101"). If no substring has exactly k ones, return an empty string.

examples.why: "1001", "101" and "11" all hold two ones. "11" is the shortest.
Both "1011" (start) and "1101" (end) have length 4. At the second character, 0 beats 1.
There is only one 1 in the string.

hints: A shortest window with exactly k ones never starts or ends with a 0: trimming it keeps k ones and makes it shorter.
So every candidate runs from some 1 to the k-th 1 after it. With the positions of all ones in a list, each candidate is one index pair.
Find the minimal length over pos[i + k − 1] − pos[i] + 1, then compare only the candidates of that length as strings.

explain.intuition:
If a window with exactly k ones starts or ends with a 0, cutting that 0 off keeps k ones and makes it shorter. So the shortest windows start on a 1 and end on a 1, with k ones in total. That means each candidate is fixed by which 1 it starts at: it runs from the i-th one to the (i + k − 1)-th one.

Collect the positions of all ones, slide a window of k consecutive positions over that list, and you get every candidate in order. Keep the shortest; on a tie in length, compare the two substrings directly. Equal-length strings compare correctly with plain string comparison.
steps: Collect pos, the indices of every 1 in s. If there are fewer than k, return "".
For each i from 0 to pos.length − k, the candidate is s.slice(pos[i], pos[i + k − 1] + 1).
Keep the candidate if it is shorter than the best so far, or the same length and smaller as a string.
pitfalls: Returning the first shortest window found instead of the smallest one among equally short windows.
Comparing candidates of different lengths as strings first. Length decides before alphabetical order: "11" beats "101" even though "101" < "11".
Including leading or trailing zeros in a window, which makes it longer than needed.

complexity.time: O(n · L) where L is the best length, at most O(n²)

solutions.title: Check every substring
solutions.idea: Try every start and end, count ones, and keep the best window with exactly k ones by length, then by string order.

solutions.title: Window over positions of ones
solutions.idea: Every shortest candidate runs from one 1 to the k-th 1 after it. Slide over the list of positions.

followups: The string has length 10^6. How do you compare tied candidates faster than character by character? (Hint: hashing or a suffix array.)
Return the number of substrings with exactly k ones instead.
lcTitle: Shortest and Lexicographically Smallest Beautiful String
